queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the very large, completely hollow bole with two straight fluted branches rising from it, and a notice naming it among the oldest yews. It stands north-west of St Giles's church.
queue.story:
A gazetteer once gave this yew 3,000 years, and the Ancient Yew Group calls that figure unsupported. A notice at the tree claims a place among the twelve oldest yews, which the group says is possible but unlisted. A published book on the trees of Sussex goes a step less far and regards it as the county's senior veteran yew.

The measured facts are impressive enough. It was 10.49 metres round fifteen centimetres off the ground in 1999, 34 feet 5 inches by the tape. A second visit in 2012 got the identical 34 feet 5 inches, and 30 feet 9 inches at three feet up. A 1997 record makes it 14 metres tall.

queue.recognise: Two veteran oaks are reported near the Motte and sources disagree about which carries the name. Look for the vast hollow one, just under nine metres round, with very little live crown left.
queue.story:
In the winter of 2016 a ranger counted the acorns on this oak. There were six, and he called that remarkable, because the tree by then barely had enough branches and twigs left to make them. Dan Clarke, senior ranger for the Lagan Valley Regional Park, put it at more than 400 years old and said outright that its condition made an exact age impossible. He measured the girth at just under nine metres.

Other authorities go higher. DAERA, the department that manages the forest, calls it the oldest living oak in Ireland at 500 to 600 years, dating it to the 1500s, and fronted a photography exhibition with it here in 2023. The Ancient Tree Forum settles on about 500.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its evergreen leaves, a Mediterranean holm oak still in leaf when its neighbours are bare, and by the low base it was once coppiced to. It stands in Fulham Palace Gardens, free and open daily.
queue.story: This oak survived five centuries partly because people kept attacking it. It was coppiced long ago, cut back hard to its base, a brutal-looking practice that paradoxically resets a tree's age clock and can add centuries to its life rather than shorten it. What grew back is a Holm Oak, an evergreen Mediterranean species that has no business thriving this far north, and quite possibly the oldest specimen of its kind anywhere in Britain. It grows in the grounds of Fulham Palace, for centuries the working home of the Bishop of London rather than a royal estate, and the two bishops most often credited with planting it, Edmund Grindal and John Aylmer, both lived here in the second half of the 16th
queue.name: The Fulham Palace Oak

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the small Great Trees of London plaque at its foot, which calls it simply the oldest plane in London. It stands at Barn Elms, on the edge of the land beside the London Wetland Centre.
queue.story: The biggest London plane in the city is a tree most Londoners have never heard of. Nicknamed Barney, it stands at Barn Elms in the riverside suburb of Barnes, tucked at the edge of the land next to the London Wetland Centre, and it is old enough, over 300 years, that it is treated locally as potentially the single oldest London plane anywhere in the capital. The species is the city's signature tree for a reason. It tolerates soot, survives brutal pruning, and outlives almost everything planted around it, and Barney is the patriarch of them all in Barnes. queue.name: Barney the Plane

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by being the only tree on Argyle Street, an ash about 23 metres tall that rises above the tenement behind it. It stands in the small front garden strip outside 1223 Argyle Street, at Franklin Terrace.
queue.story:
The only tree on Argyle Street arrived by accident, in the roots of a primrose. In the 1850s the first residents of a new tenement at Franklin Terrace came back from holiday with primroses for their scrap of front garden, and an ash seed came with them in the soil. Nobody wrote down the year, so its age of roughly 175 years is counted from that story rather than from a ring.

By 1951, when James Cowan described it in From Glasgow's Treasure Chest, it stood 75 feet tall, about 23 metres, and had outgrown the building that planted it without meaning to. queue.recognise: A trunk about twenty metres round at the base splitting into more than three hundred branches, standing alone in the park that was laid out around it in 1996.
queue.story: Nobody can date this tree, and nobody is going to. Dracaena draco lays down no annual growth rings, so the standard method of reading a trunk fails on it completely, and the estimates fill the vacuum accordingly: current scientific work puts El Drago Milenario near 700 years with a margin of a century or more either way, while tradition, the tourist literature and the tree's own name insist on a thousand or more. The name is a claim, not a measurement. What can actually be measured is everything else. queue.name: El Drago Milenario

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the swollen, knobbled trunk under a crown far too small for it. It stands south of the lower grassy area in Ravenscourt Park, near the elm avenue, about 150 metres from the park's tree of heaven.
queue.story: A virus is the best explanation anyone has for the shape of this tree. It carries a swollen, knobbled trunk under a crown far too small for it, the signature of the rare Baobab group of London plane, a form believed to come from viral infection rather than ordinary growth. Few are known; the closest comparable specimens grow in Canterbury. Nobody can say how old it is, and the sources sit far apart. A specialist plane blog puts its planting somewhere in the nineteenth century, so 150 to 225 years.
